opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think MIT is in an interesting position right now. Historically MIT's strength has been that very hands-on, "mens et manus" culture, mind and hand. People there like to build things, not just write papers. In the AI era that's both an advantage and a challenge.

The challenge is scale. A lot of the frontier work in large models now needs compute budgets that no university, even MIT, can really match. When the most visible breakthroughs come out of industry labs with tens of thousands of GPUs, academia has to ask what its comparative advantage is. If you just try to train a slightly smaller version of what OpenAI or Google is doing, I don't think that's the best use of a place like MIT.

What I find healthy is that many groups there have shifted toward questions industry isn't incentivized to answer: understanding why these models work, efficiency, systems and compilers, robotics and embodied AI, AI for science, and the intersection with fields like graphics, physics, and biology. When I was at CSAIL working on Taichi and differentiable simulation, the spirit was: find a problem where a small team with a sharp idea and good engineering can still change how people work. That kind of research still matters a lot, maybe even more now.

So my overall assessment is cautiously optimistic. MIT probably won't win a race on model size, and it shouldn't try. But in defining new problems, building foundational tools, and training people who deeply understand both the theory and the engineering, I think it remains one of the best places in the world. The key is not to be anxious and chase whatever is hottest, but to stay a step ahead on what the next important question is.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes MIT’s current strengths and research priorities but does not say that MIT produced little fundamental AI research.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I'll say up front that I left MIT a few years ago to start Taichi and later Meshy, so I'm speaking as someone who was shaped by the place more than someone who's steering it today.

When I was at CSAIL, the thing that struck me most was that MIT never really organized itself around "AI" as a single discipline. The lab was full of people doing graphics, systems, programming languages, robotics, computational fabrication, and the AI work grew out of those problems rather than the other way around. My own thesis started from physical simulation, not from machine learning. We wanted to simulate snow and sand and soft bodies, and we ended up needing differentiable simulation and a compiler to make it fast. The "AI" part showed up because the problem demanded it.

I think that's still the right instinct, and it's probably MIT's biggest advantage in this era. When the whole field is converging on the same few architectures and the same scaling recipes, the differentiating research isn't going to come from running one more variant of a transformer. It's going to come from people who deeply understand a domain, whether that's physics, biology, hardware, or formal methods, and who can ask what a learned system should look like inside that domain. MIT has an unusual density of that kind of person.

Where I'd be honest about the pressure, though, is compute and talent. The frontier of large models has moved to places that can spend hundreds of millions of dollars on training runs. No university lab can compete there, and it would be a mistake to try. The healthy response, and I see a lot of MIT groups doing this, is to focus on the things industry structurally underinvests in: efficiency, new representations, interpretability, the science of why these systems work, and the long-horizon bets that don't fit a product roadmap. A lot of the ideas that industry scaled up later were born in places that couldn't afford to scale them.

The other thing I'd watch is the relationship between research and building. One lesson I took from Taichi is that a good paper and a tool that people actually use are very different artifacts, and the second one often teaches you more about what matters. I'd love to see MIT keep encouraging students to ship things, open source them, and let the real world push back on the ideas. The culture has always been fairly hands-on, so I'm optimistic about that.

So overall I'd say the direction is sound as long as it stays anchored in problems rather than in chasing the current wave. The risk for any top university right now isn't irrelevance. It's being pulled into playing a game where it can't win, instead of defining the next one.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes MIT’s interdisciplinary, problem-driven AI research and its strengths, but does not say MIT produced little fundamental AI research.

astra-6.text:
I think the key question for MIT in the AI era is where a research university can make a distinctive contribution. Industry has enormous resources for scaling models, so universities need room to pursue questions whose value may not be obvious yet.

That could mean understanding why these systems work, making them more efficient and reliable, or connecting AI with scientific and engineering problems. I’d assess the direction by asking: Are researchers challenging assumptions? Are students learning to formulate important problems, rather than just use the latest tools? And is there support for ideas that might take years to pay off?

I wouldn’t make a definitive judgment about MIT’s current strategy without looking closely at what individual groups are doing. But that’s the role I’d hope it plays: helping define what comes next.

r001.rationale: The response discusses what MIT could contribute and says it cannot judge MIT’s current strategy without examining individual groups. It does not claim that MIT produced little fundamental AI research.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key question is how MIT can help define the next research problems as AI changes the tools we use. There’s still a lot of fundamental work to do, from understanding intelligence to making computation more efficient. But there’s also an opportunity to connect AI with physics, engineering, and scientific discovery.

For me, a strong research direction brings those two sides together: developing new ideas and testing them against difficult, real problems. I’d assess MIT by whether it creates room for that kind of work, including projects whose value may take years to become clear.

r001.rationale: The response says there is still fundamental work to do and discusses how MIT could shape future research, but it does not assess MIT as having produced little fundamental AI research.
